e.t: This word means “purity,” describing a condition free from moral corruption or mixed motives. It refers to inward cleanness that can shape a person’s conduct, intentions, and faithfulness. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs two times, both in 2 Corinthians. The word’s basic sense is broad enough to describe sincerity and moral integrity, but its precise force in either verse depends on the surrounding context. It points readers toward what is clean and undivided rather than polluted or deceptive.

This word means “street,” referring to a public way or roadway. It is a noun used to identify a place or route rather than an action, person, or quality. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in Mark 11:4. The word’s precise role in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its ordinary meaning remains a street or roadway. This is a straightforward location word with a single recorded New Testament occurrence.

This word means “to bring back” or “to restore.” It is a verb describing the act of returning someone or something to an earlier condition or position. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in Hebrews 6:6. That occurrence establishes its basic action, while the surrounding passage is needed to determine exactly what is being restored or brought back there. Its central idea is renewal through return, rather than simply introducing something new.

This word refers to a bucket or other container used to draw water. It names the vessel itself, not the action of drawing. In the Greek New Testament, it appears once, at John 4:11, in a conversation about obtaining water from a well. The word therefore has a practical, everyday sense: a container carried or lowered for collecting water. Its precise significance in that verse depends on the surrounding passage and the speaker’s situation.

e.t: This New Testament verb means “to touch” or “to kindle.” It describes making contact with something or someone, and it can also express setting something alight or stirring it into flame. The word occurs 39 times in the Greek New Testament, so its exact force depends on the sentence in which it appears. In many passages, its ordinary sense is physical contact, while “to kindle” reflects its use for producing or igniting fire. [p03:word:greek-nt:G0681:identity] [p03:word:greek-nt:G0681:occurrences]

Artemis is the name of a named figure referred to in the Greek New Testament. It is not a general quality, action, or description, but a personal name used as a designation. This word occurs five times in the Greek New Testament, all within Acts 19, and each occurrence is rendered “Artemis.” It appears in Acts 19:24, 27, 28, 34, and 35. The precise significance of each mention belongs to its surrounding verse and passage.

e.t: This word means “nearer,” indicating that someone or something is closer than before or closer in comparison with another position. It points to increased nearness rather than distance. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in Acts 27:13. Its exact force in that verse depends on the surrounding sentence and passage, but its basic meaning remains a movement or position toward greater closeness.

This word means “imperishableness,” “incorruptibility,” or “integrity”—the quality of remaining free from decay, corruption, or moral failure. It describes something enduring and sound rather than temporary or spoiled. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs eight times across eight verses, including several passages in 1 Corinthians 15 that use this idea in connection with what is not subject to decay. Its precise emphasis in a particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence.

e.t: This Greek New Testament word means “to torture”: to inflict severe suffering on someone. It describes an action rather than a person or object, and its basic sense is direct and forceful. The word occurs 12 times in the Greek New Testament, appearing in twelve verses. Its exact force in any particular passage depends on the surrounding verse and situation, but the central idea remains the deliberate infliction of painful suffering.

This word means a “cry” or “outcry”—a vocal expression that calls attention to a pressing need, distress, or demand. It points to the sound or appeal itself rather than explaining the surrounding situation. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs only once, in James 5:4. Its precise force there must be understood from the verse and its surrounding passage, but the word itself describes an audible cry raised for others to hear.

Timidity means a shrinking, hesitant lack of confidence or boldness. It describes an inward disposition rather than an outward action, naming the quality of being timid. In the Greek New Testament, this word occurs once, at 2 Timothy 1:7. The lexical sense is clear, while the word’s precise force in that verse belongs to the surrounding sentence and passage itself.

This Greek New Testament word means “public,” describing something done openly or before people rather than privately. It functions as an adverb, showing the manner or setting of an action. The word occurs four times in the Greek New Testament, all in Acts, where it qualifies actions carried out openly. Its basic sense is straightforward: what is public is visible or accessible to others, in contrast with what is hidden or restricted to private settings.

e.t: This word means “to doubt,” describing uncertainty or hesitation rather than settled confidence. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs twice, both times in Matthew. Its basic sense is to question or waver inwardly, though the exact force in either verse depends on the surrounding passage. The word appears in Matthew 14:31 and Matthew 28:17, but those references alone do not establish the full contextual emphasis.

This word refers to an “idol's temple” or “temple of an idol”—a place associated with the worship of an idol. It identifies the location itself rather than the idol or the act of worship. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in 1 Corinthians 8:10. Its precise significance in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and context, but its basic meaning remains a temple connected with an idol.

This word means “olive oil,” the oil produced from olives. It is a concrete noun referring to a familiar substance used in ordinary life and in several biblical settings. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs 11 times, including references involving lamps, anointing, and care for the injured. Its basic meaning remains the same across these uses; the surrounding passage determines how the oil functions in a particular verse.

e.h: A Greek Woman or Greek Person
e.t: This word refers to a Greek person, and can specifically identify a Greek woman. It is a people-designating term, describing someone as Greek rather than naming an action, quality, or object. Within the Greek New Testament, it occurs twice, in Mark 7:26 and Acts 17:12. Its precise reference in either verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic meaning is someone identified as Greek.

This word is the personal name “Enosh,” referring to a person rather than describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek New Testament, it appears once, at Luke 3:38. Because it is a proper name, its meaning is chiefly identifying: it distinguishes one person from others rather than expressing a broader idea that can be applied to many situations. Its precise significance in that verse depends on the surrounding passage.

This word refers to a north wind, specifically a northeast wind. It names a wind direction or type rather than expressing an action, quality, or person. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in Acts 27:14. Because the verse text and surrounding passage are not included here, its precise force in that scene cannot be described from the lexical meaning alone. Its central sense remains a particular wind coming from the north or northeast.

This word means an animal, especially a wild animal. It is a noun used to refer to living creatures rather than people, and its exact force depends on the surrounding sentence. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs 46 times, with most occurrences in Revelation. There it is repeatedly used for creatures described as animals or wild animals, while other occurrences refer more generally to an animal. The central idea remains a living creature of the animal kind, with context showing whether the emphasis is simply on an animal or on its wild character.

This word describes someone as “reverent”—a person who shows deep respect and honor, especially toward what is sacred. It presents reverence as a recognizable quality of a person’s character and conduct, rather than merely a private feeling. The word occurs once in the Greek New Testament, in Titus 2:3. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic meaning is someone characterized by reverence.

e.t: This word means “to stay,” describing remaining in a place rather than leaving. It is a verb that focuses on continuing to be present. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in Acts 1:13. Its exact force in that verse depends on the surrounding sentence and passage, but its basic sense is continued presence or remaining where one is. It does not by itself explain the reason for staying; the context supplies that detail.

This word refers to an accusation or charge brought against a person. It describes a claim that someone has done something wrong and may be presented for examination or judgment. As a noun, it names the accusation itself rather than the act of making it. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs three times, so its basic sense remains consistent across its limited use. The surrounding passage determines what the charge concerns in any particular verse.

e.t: This Greek New Testament word means to bow down or lay something down. It can describe a person lowering or bending down, or an action of placing something in a lower position. The central idea is a movement downward, whether expressed as “bowed,” “to bow,” or “to lay down.” It occurs seven times in the Greek New Testament, so its precise sense in any verse depends on what is being lowered or laid down there.

This word refers to “oracles” or “words”—spoken messages treated as a significant verbal communication. It functions as a plural noun, naming words or utterances rather than an action or quality. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs four times, so its meaning is established across several passages rather than being limited to one occurrence. The exact force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence and passage.

e.t: This word means “hardly” or “with difficulty,” describing something that happens only with struggle, limitation, or a narrow possibility. It can express that an action is barely accomplished or that an outcome is not easily expected. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs six times, including descriptions of difficult travel and statements emphasizing how uncommon or difficult something is. Its exact force depends on the sentence, but the central idea remains clear: what happens does not happen readily or easily.

This word means “form” or “embodiment”: the outward expression or concrete shape of something. It can describe an expressed form rather than merely an idea, helping identify how something is presented or made visible. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs twice, in Romans 2:20 and 2 Timothy 3:5. Its precise force in either passage depends on the surrounding sentence, but its central sense remains an expressed form or embodiment.

This word refers to strips or bands of linen used as cloth wrappings. Its meaning is concrete and ordinary: narrow pieces of linen, rather than linen as a material in general. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs five times, all in Luke 24 and John 19–20. The references place it among descriptions of linen connected with Jesus’ burial and the tomb, but the word itself names the cloth strips or bandages, not the wider event or its significance.

This word means a vision or visions—a sight or revelation perceived in a special way. It is a noun used for visionary experiences rather than ordinary physical seeing. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs four times, referring generally to experiences described as visions. Its precise significance in any particular passage depends on the surrounding verse and context, but the central idea remains a vision granted or experienced beyond normal observation.

This word means “by the lake” or “seaside,” describing a location beside a body of water. It functions as a place-related expression rather than naming a person, object, or action. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs only once, in Matthew 4:13. The word identifies the general setting associated with the place mentioned there, while the surrounding verse and passage provide the fuller context. Its basic meaning is geographical: it points to an area along the shore or beside a lake.

me: ADVerb or adverb and particle combined

e.t: This word means “momentary,” describing something that lasts only for a brief moment rather than an extended period. It points to short duration and helps distinguish what is temporary from what continues. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in 2 Corinthians 4:17. Its basic meaning is limited to the duration being described; the surrounding verse determines what temporary matter is in view. This word therefore draws attention to brevity, emphasizing that something is brief in comparison with what lasts longer.

e.t: This word means “to try.” It describes making an attempt to do something, rather than simply thinking about it or intending it. As a verb, it expresses an action of trying within a sentence. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in Acts 26:21. The precise force of that attempt in the verse depends on the surrounding passage, but the word itself centers on undertaking an effort or making an attempt.

This Greek New Testament word means “but” or “however.” It is a conjunction, so it links words, phrases, or statements by setting one idea in contrast with, or qualification beside, another. Its force is usually connective rather than descriptive: it helps the reader follow a turn in the argument or a limitation on what has just been said. It occurs 31 times in the Greek New Testament, from Matthew through Revelation. The surrounding verse determines whether “but” or “however” best expresses the contrast.

me: ADVerb or adverb and particle combined

e.t: This Greek adverb means “richly.” It describes something given, supplied, or carried out in a full and abundant way, showing that the action is not slight or limited. In the Greek New Testament, it appears four times, each time emphasizing the generous extent of what is being described. Its exact force in a particular verse depends on the action or subject it modifies, but its central idea remains abundance rather than scarcity.

Porcius is a personal name, referring to an individual named Porcius rather than describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek New Testament, it appears once, in Acts 24:27. The English Bible preserves the name as “Porcius,” so its meaning is primarily its role as a proper name identifying a person. The surrounding verse context would be needed to explain that person’s particular role there.

e.t: This word means “foreseeing”—seeing or knowing something beforehand. It describes awareness of what is going to happen before the event occurs, rather than merely seeing it at the present moment. In the Greek New Testament, it appears four times, including passages in Acts and Galatians. Its precise force in any individual verse depends on the surrounding sentence and passage, but its central idea remains seeing previously or anticipating what lies ahead.

Sapphira is a personal name, referring to a person named Sapphira rather than describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek New Testament, it appears once, in Acts 5:1, and is rendered as “Sapphira.” Because it is a name, its basic meaning is identification: it tells the reader who a person is called, while the surrounding verse supplies the specific context of that person’s role in the passage.

This word means “soldier” or “soldiers,” referring to people serving in an organized military force. It is a noun used for individual troops or soldiers considered as a group. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs 26 times in 24 verses, including passages mentioning soldiers in the accounts of Jesus’ ministry, crucifixion, burial, and resurrection. Its precise role in any particular verse depends on the surrounding context.

This word refers to music or musical sound. It is a noun describing music itself rather than a person, action, or quality. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in Luke 15:25, and its meaning is rendered “music.” The word therefore identifies the audible musical element mentioned in that passage. Its precise significance in the verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic meaning is clear: music.

This word means “tavern,” referring to a public place where people gather for food, drink, and fellowship. It is a noun naming a physical meeting place rather than an action, quality, or person. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs only once, in Acts 28:15. The word itself identifies the kind of place mentioned; the surrounding verse and passage are needed to understand what happened there and why it is mentioned.

This word means “bull” or “bulls,” referring to the large male animal. It is a noun used for bulls as animals, including those mentioned in sacrificial settings. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs four times, appearing in Matthew, Acts, and Hebrews. Its precise role in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic meaning remains the same: a bull or multiple bulls.

e.t: The Greek New Testament word means “to gnash,” describing the forceful grinding or striking together of the teeth. It is a verb, so it names an action rather than a person, object, or quality. This word occurs once in the Greek New Testament, at Mark 9:18. Its precise force in that verse is best understood from the surrounding passage, but its basic meaning remains the act of gnashing.

me: Verb, Aorist, Active, Participle, Nominative, Singular, Masculine

e.t: This word means “to flog” or “to whip”—to strike a person repeatedly with a whip as punishment. It is a verb describing the act itself, rather than the person carrying it out or the instrument used. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs twice: at Matthew 27:26 and Mark 15:15. Its basic meaning remains the physical act of flogging or whipping, while the surrounding verse determines its precise force in each sentence.

This word means an image or mark: something made or placed as a recognizable representation or identifying sign. It is a noun describing a visible mark or image rather than an action. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs eight times, once in Acts and seven times in Revelation. Its meaning can therefore refer broadly to an image, while its precise significance in a particular passage depends on the surrounding words and context.

me: Verb, Future, Active, Indicative, third, Plural

e.t: This Greek New Testament word means “to build” or “to encamp.” It describes constructing something or setting up a camp, giving the idea of establishing a place or position. It appears once in the Greek New Testament, in Luke 19:43. The surrounding verse determines which sense is intended there, but the word itself centers on building or establishing an encampment. Its meaning therefore concerns either construction or the organized placement of a camp.
